Summary: The paper proposes CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that treats the site (hospital) rather than the record as the unit of independence. Each calibration site is reduced to a bounded atom Z_c built from an influence-capped (M=100) answered-set error, and a Waudby-Smith–Ramdas betting martingale tests whether the site-population mean of that atom exceeds a budget α; a fixed-sequence (learn-then-test style) walk over a 23-point threshold grid, ordered on a separate auxiliary split, selects the operating threshold without δ-splitting, and two budget rungs α∈{0.05,0.10} are combined at 1−2δ. Two assumption modes are shipped and named in the guarantee text: an exchangeable baseline and a BBSE label-shift mode whose four estimated parameters carry cluster-bootstrap/Clopper–Pearson uncertainty into a ρ box tested at both endpoints. Because the head is L2 logistic regression, answers and abstentions carry exact additive attributions and a margin-to-answer decomposition; a three-way answered-set composition disclosure is reported beside the certificate. On a 208-site synthetic cohort (E1–E7) the α=0.10 rung certifies all 200 draws at 0.98 coverage with zero exceedances of the certified estimand, α=0.05 is unreachable below ~300 sites, the uncorrected baseline certifies-and-violates 39.5% under a prevalence shift while BBSE declines all draws, a verified concept-shift negative control fails as excluded, and a record-as-unit comparator violates its budget at up to ~2δ. On eICU-CRD v2.0 (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol frozen before the extract was read, α=0.10 certifies on all 20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 mean coverage, α=0.05 on none, with no exceedance on held-out 24-hospital pools; the authors disclose that the answered set's mortality (0.046) is about half the pool's (0.090).
Strengths: Addresses a real and under-served problem: record-level selective-risk certificates are overconfident under site-clustered deployment, and clinical multi-site data is the canonical case.

The core construction is technically sound as far as I can verify: the atom Z_c is bounded in [0,1] with E[Z] ≤ α iff R_M ≤ α, the capped predictable bet keeps the wealth process a nonnegative supermartingale under H0, Ville's inequality gives δ, the threshold ordering is computed on a disjoint auxiliary split so the fixed-sequence walk spends no extra confidence, and the two rungs are Bonferroni-combined.

Unusually candid reporting: the guarantee text explicitly names what is not bounded (per-site risk, realized counts, concept shift), a verified-falsifiable negative control and a record-as-unit comparator are run on the same draws, and the composition/skill disclosures on eICU show the gate earning part of its budget by abstaining where deaths concentrate.

The eICU study is run under a protocol with cohort predicates, feature allowlist, leak denylist, seven predictions and five failure criteria committed before the extract was read; falsified predictions are reported as falsified, and leak screens (including one that fired in the opposite direction) are documented.
Reproducibility is strong: released code, deterministic seeding, constants pinned by tests, byte-identical certificates, and an aggregate-only release policy for the restricted data.
The influence-cap sensitivity sweep (M from 25 to 5000) and the site-count frontier (E4) give useful capacity-planning information.
Weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited for a prestigious ML venue. The certificate is a direct composition of existing tools — WSR betting for bounded means [7], cluster-as-unit atoms [24,25], fixed-sequence LTT [9,10], BBSE [13,14], and the uncertainty-in-the-guarantee pattern of [15]. The paper itself frames the contribution as drawing on four literatures; the new content is the specific atom Z_c and the surrounding engineering/disclosure apparatus rather than a new statistical idea.

The certified quantity is nearly vacuous at the only achievable rung. At 8.9–9.5% prevalence an always-negative rule already meets α=0.10 (0.1039 error on the synthetic pools; 0.089 on eICU), and the paper's own post-hoc panel reports an answered-set skill margin over that trivial rule of only 0.0039 on eICU. α=0.05 is unreachable at realistic site counts, and even it sits near the answered set's trivial-rule error (0.046). The paper acknowledges this, but it means the headline certificate carries little clinical content.

The guarantee is a site-population average, so a deploying hospital receives no bound for itself; on eICU one hospital ran at 0.29 answered error under a valid certificate. The paper is honest about this, but it sharply limits the practical significance of the 'certificate' for the cross-institutional deployment scenario that motivates the work.

The label-shift mode is shown to be safe but essentially never useful: it declines all 200 draws at the anchor shift, certifies 9% at the null shift, and on eICU fits a ρ box of [0.068, 1.986] and certifies nothing. Three of its four intervals are asymptotic bootstraps with measured joint miscoverage 0.038 vs nominal ≤0.019, so the 'finite-sample' claim strictly applies only to the exchangeable mode. Contribution 2 is therefore weakly evidenced.

No comparison to simpler or alternative cluster-level procedures. With ~83 site atoms and a fixed sequence (no optional stopping across sites), it is unclear what the betting martingale buys over a one-sided cluster-level empirical-Bernstein/Hoeffding or t-based bound; nor is there any empirical comparison to hierarchical/cluster conformal risk control [24–27] on the same draws or on eICU. The only comparator is the record-as-unit version of the authors' own machinery.

The record-as-unit comparator's failure is modest: at α=0.10 it does not violate (fresh-pool risk 0.081), and at α=0.05 the violation is 3.5% and 9.6% at the two heterogeneity arms — the 'motivating failure' is demonstrated only at one rung in the more heterogeneous arm.

The synthetic harness is easy (8 features, linear signal, well-specified logistic head, 0.98 coverage) so the validity results largely restate what the martingale theorem guarantees; the head is a simple L2 logistic regression and the model-agnostic claim (coverage cost of a stronger head) is asserted, not tested.

The explainability contribution is thin: exact attributions for a linear model are coefficient × centered feature, margin-to-answer is a direct corollary, and E5 returns a null on the synthetic generator.

The equity analysis is by site size only; there is no patient-subgroup analysis (age, sex, race, admission type) on eICU even though abstention concentrates on sicker patients, which is exactly where differential deferral could matter.

Symmetric 0–1 loss with ~77% of answered errors being false negatives is a poor match to mortality/deterioration triage; the authors defer a cost-weighted atom to future work, but this further reduces the clinical meaning of the bounded quantity.

Presentation: the writing is dense, self-referential and idiosyncratic ('rung', 'walk', 'atom', 'failsafe', 'poison', 'honest'), with long disclosure passages and very long table captions; the method is hard to extract on first read and the paper reads more like a protocol/audit report than a research paper. A compact algorithm box and a formal theorem statement for the exchangeable guarantee would help considerably.
Questions: What does the betting martingale add over a one-sided empirical-Bernstein / Hoeffding / t-based bound computed on the ~83 site atoms Z_c, given that the walk is a fixed sequence over thresholds and there is no optional stopping over sites? Please report certify rates and coverage under such a simpler cluster-level test on the same draws.

Given that an always-negative rule already meets α=0.10 at this prevalence, what does the certificate tell a deployer? Can the framework certify a quantity that is not trivially satisfied — e.g., a bound on answered false-negative rate, or a cost-weighted risk — and what does that cost in coverage or site count?

Is there any realistic configuration (synthetic or real) where the BBSE mode certifies a materially useful fraction of draws under a genuine shift? On eICU the ρ box was [0.068, 1.986]; how many auxiliary/target sites would be needed to bring it to a usable width?

How should the 1−δ guarantee be interpreted on eICU, where the 74 calibration hospitals are a random subset of a fixed finite population of 207 and the target is the complement? Does Assumption 1 hold in a finite-population sense, and is any correction warranted?
Please compare, at least empirically, against hierarchical/cluster conformal risk control [24–27] on the synthetic grid to place the coverage cost of the high-probability answered-set guarantee.
What is the coverage cost when the linear head is replaced by a stronger non-linear model (e.g., gradient boosting) on eICU? The paper claims model-agnosticism but does not show it.
How sensitive are the eICU and E4 results to the 50 record-carrying-cluster floor and the 10-record answerable floor?

Does deferral concentrate on identifiable patient subgroups on eICU (age, sex, race, admission source)? A subgroup breakdown of coverage and answered error would materially strengthen the equity claim.
Limitations: The authors are unusually forthcoming: site-population-average scope, no per-site bound, no concept-shift protection, symmetric loss, asymptotic BBSE intervals, temporal common shocks, one real cohort with 20 re-splits, and the answered set being easier than its pool are all stated.

Not adequately addressed: (a) the certificate's clinical content when α is at or above prevalence — a deployer could read 'certified at α=0.10' as assurance when the trivial rule already meets it; (b) the risk that a 'certificate' gives false assurance at the individual-hospital level (a hospital at 0.29 answered error sat under a valid one), which is a plausible negative societal impact if such certificates are used in procurement or regulatory settings; (c) fairness beyond site size — abstention concentrates on sicker patients and no patient-subgroup analysis is given, so differential deferral by demographic group is unexamined; (d) workload shift to clinicians from deferral of the highest-risk cases is not discussed.
